tool.name: XGBoost
tool.tagline: Fast, regularised gradient-boosted trees for tabular data
tool.description: XGBoost is an optimised gradient boosting library that builds ensembles of decision trees using second-order gradients and built-in regularisation. It handles missing values and categorical features natively, scales from a laptop to GPUs and clusters, and offers both a scikit-learn compatible API and a lower-level native API. It is one of the strongest and most widely used models for tabular prediction tasks.

glossary.def: A scikit-learn tool that turns class names such as "cat" and "dog" into the integers 0, 1, 2... and turns predictions back into names with inverse_transform.
In XGBoost, the loss it minimises while training, chosen by a name such as "reg:squarederror" or "binary:logistic". The part before the colon names the kind of task.
A score for predicted probabilities that punishes confident mistakes hard: predicting 99% for something that turns out false costs far more than predicting 60%. Lower is better.
A choice of loss for counts, such as visits per day or claims per year: it assumes the counts vary around an average that is never negative.
A choice of loss for amounts that are often exactly zero and otherwise positive, such as insurance claims per customer.
One step of gradient boosting, in which one more tree is added (one per class for multi-class problems). The number of rounds is the number of trees.
The branch, left or right, that a tree split sends a row to when the row's value for that feature is missing. XGBoost learns it during training by trying both sides.
Universal Binary JSON: the same structure as JSON, stored as compact bytes instead of readable text, so files are smaller and load faster.
XGBoost's own data holder: your features, plus the answers and optional extras such as row weights, converted once into the form XGBoost trains on.
A DMatrix that stores only which bin (value range) each value falls into, not the value itself, so it uses much less memory.
One of the value ranges a feature is cut into (at most 256 by default). XGBoost only tries split points between bins, which makes finding splits much faster.
XGBoost's trained model in its native interface: all the trees plus their settings. The scikit-learn style classes keep one inside, returned by get_booster().
A way of writing a probability p as log(p / (1 - p)): 0 means 50%, positive means more likely yes, negative more likely no. The sigmoid turns it back into a probability.
A rule that a feature may only push predictions one way: as the feature rises, predictions never go down (or never go up), with the other features held fixed.
A rule listing which groups of features may be used together along one tree branch; features from different groups then never interact.
When one feature's effect depends on another's value, such as a discount mattering only for new customers. A tree captures it by splitting on one feature and then on the other.
Training a model to put items in the best order for each search or user, rather than predicting a number or class for each item on its own.
In ranking, one search or one user visit that comes with a list of candidate items to put in order. Items are only compared with others from the same query.
A ranking score from 0 to 1, where 1 is the perfect order. Mistakes near the top cost more than mistakes lower down; NDCG@10 looks only at the first 10 positions.
People click top results partly just because they are on top, so clicks make top-placed items look better than they are.
The second derivative of the loss: how quickly its slope (the gradient) changes as a prediction moves. Boosting libraries use it to decide how big each leaf's correction should be.
The plain sum of a boosted model's tree outputs, before it is turned into a prediction. For a yes/no classifier it is the log-odds, which the sigmoid turns into a probability.
The function that turns a model's raw margin into the prediction you see: the sigmoid for probabilities, or exp for counts (a log link).
NVIDIA's system for running general calculations on its GPUs. device="cuda" tells a library to train on an NVIDIA GPU.
Training on data that stays on disk and is read in batches, so the dataset can be bigger than RAM.
Apache Spark: a system for processing very large datasets by splitting the work across many machines in a cluster.
A step in which many machines combine their partial results, such as adding up their histograms, so every machine ends up with the same total.

concepts.name: XGBoost with the scikit-learn API
concepts.summary: Train XGBClassifier and XGBRegressor exactly like scikit-learn estimators.
concepts.why: The scikit-learn-style classes are the quickest way to use XGBoost, and scikit-learn's own tools work with them.
concepts.body:
A single decision tree is easy to read but rarely very accurate. **Gradient boosting** gets accuracy through teamwork: it builds trees one after another, and each new tree is trained to fix the mistakes the trees before it still make. To predict, it adds up the outputs of all the trees. Think of students correcting a piece of homework in turn: each one only has to fix what is still wrong.

XGBoost is a library that does gradient boosting quickly and with extra safeguards against overfitting. It is one of the most accurate tools for tabular data: tables of rows and columns, like a spreadsheet.

The `xgboost` package gives you estimators that behave like scikit-learn's:

- `XGBClassifier` for classification, with two classes or more,
- `XGBRegressor` for regression,
- `XGBRanker` for putting items in order, such as search results (a later lesson).

You use them the familiar way: hyperparameters in the constructor, then `fit(X, y)`, `predict(X)`, `predict_proba(X)` and `score`. X can be a NumPy array or a pandas DataFrame; with a DataFrame the model remembers the column names. Because they follow scikit-learn's rules, scikit-learn's tools for splitting, scoring and comparing models accept them too.

The defaults are reasonable: 100 trees (`n_estimators`), a learning rate of 0.3 (how much each new tree may change the prediction; see Core hyperparameters) and trees at most 6 questions deep (`max_depth`). Unlike linear models or k-NN, trees need **no feature scaling**: a tree only asks "is this value above a cut-off?", so stretching a column changes nothing. Missing values (`NaN`) are allowed too; a later lesson explains how.

For classification, the labels must be the integers 0, 1, 2 and so on. Text labels such as `"spam"` raise an error, so turn them into numbers first with scikit-learn's `LabelEncoder`, and turn predictions back with its `inverse_transform`.
concepts.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from xgboost import XGBClassifier

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=0)

model = XGBClassifier(n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=4)
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print(round(model.score(X_te, y_te), 3))         # 0.951 (accuracy)
print(model.predict_proba(X_te.iloc[:2]).round(3))
# [[0. 1.]
#  [1. 0.]]   (very confident on these two rows)
print(model.n_features_in_, model.feature_names_in_[:2])
# 30 ['mean radius' 'mean texture']
takeaways: Gradient boosting builds trees one after another, each fixing the earlier trees' mistakes
XGBClassifier/XGBRegressor follow scikit-learn's fit/predict pattern
No feature scaling needed, and NaN is allowed
Class labels must be the integers 0, 1, 2...
pitfalls: Passing text class labels to XGBClassifier without turning them into integers first.

quiz.q: Which preprocessing step is unnecessary for XGBoost but important for logistic regression?
quiz.explain: A tree only compares values with cut-offs, so rescaling a column doesn't change which rows go where.

quiz.q: In gradient boosting, what is each new tree trained to do?
options: Predict the target on its own, independently of the others
Fix the mistakes the trees before it still make
quiz.explain: Trees are added one after another, each correcting what the sum of the earlier trees still gets wrong.

concepts.name: Objectives and evaluation metrics
concepts.summary: Choose the loss XGBoost minimises (objective) and the score it reports while training (eval_metric) for your task.
concepts.why: The objective defines what 'good' means during training; the wrong one quietly optimises the wrong thing.
concepts.body:
Every model is trained to make some score of its mistakes as small as possible. That formula is the **loss function**, and XGBoost calls the one it uses the **objective**. The scikit-learn classes pick a sensible one for you, but you can choose it with `objective=`. The part before the colon names the kind of task:

- `reg:squarederror` (the regressor's default): squared error, so big misses count a lot,
- `reg:absoluteerror`: absolute error, so a few wild values (outliers) pull the model less,
- `reg:quantileerror` with `quantile_alpha=0.9`: predicts a quantile, here a value the target stays below 90% of the time,
- `count:poisson`: for counts such as visits per day, which are never negative,
- `reg:tweedie`: for amounts that are often exactly zero, like insurance claims,
- `binary:logistic` (the yes/no classifier's default): predicts probabilities,
- `multi:softprob`: probabilities for three or more classes, chosen automatically when y has more than two classes.

The classification objectives are scored by **log loss**. It punishes confident mistakes hard: saying 99% for something that turns out false costs far more than saying 60%.

The **evaluation metric** (`eval_metric=`) is separate. It doesn't change training: it is the score XGBoost reports on data you hold aside while training. It is also what early stopping watches; that later lesson stops training once this score stops improving. Options include `rmse`, `mae`, `logloss`, `error` (the share of wrong answers), and `auc` and `aucpr`, two scores of how well a classifier puts positives above negatives. If you pass a list, early stopping uses the last one.

Pick the objective to match the kind of target and how you will use the predictions; pick the metric to match how you will judge the model. A fraud model, for example, might train with `binary:logistic` but watch `aucpr`, which suits rare positives. Afterwards, scikit-learn metrics on the test set remain the final judge.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
from xgboost import XGBRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(0, 10, size=(2000, 3))
y = rng.poisson(np.exp(0.2 * X[:, 0] - 0.1 * X[:, 1]))   # count target

sq = XGBRegressor(n_estimators=200, max_depth=3).fit(X, y)
pois = XGBRegressor(n_estimators=200, max_depth=3, objective="count:poisson").fit(X, y)

x_new = np.array([[9.0, 0.0, 5.0], [0.0, 9.0, 5.0]])
print(np.exp(0.2 * x_new[:, 0] - 0.1 * x_new[:, 1]).round(2))  # [6.05 0.41] (true averages)
print(sq.predict(x_new).round(2), pois.predict(x_new).round(2))  # [7.2  0.29] [6.9  0.27]

q90 = XGBRegressor(objective="reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha=0.9, n_estimators=200).fit(X, y)
print(round(float((y <= q90.predict(X)).mean()), 2))     # 0.92 (about 90% lie below)
takeaways: `objective` = what training minimises; `eval_metric` = what is reported and watched
Match the objective to the target: counts, quantiles, outlier-resistant errors
Classifiers pick a logistic or softprob objective automatically
pitfalls: Using squared error on a count target when `count:poisson` fits it better.

quiz.q: You need predictions that are exceeded only 10% of the time (an upper bound). Which objective fits?
quiz.explain: Quantile loss with alpha 0.9 aims at the value the target stays below 90% of the time.

quiz.q: What does changing eval_metric from 'logloss' to 'auc' change?
options: The loss the trees are fitted to
The score XGBoost reports and early stopping watches
quiz.explain: Training follows the objective; eval_metric only decides which score is reported on held-out data and monitored.

concepts.name: Core hyperparameters
concepts.summary: Understand the handful of parameters that control model capacity, learning speed and randomness.
concepts.why: Most of XGBoost's performance comes from a few parameters; knowing what each does makes tuning fast.
concepts.body:
XGBoost has dozens of settings, but a handful matter most. They control three things: how fast the model learns, how complicated each tree may get, and how much randomness goes into each tree.

**Learning rate and number of trees.** Each new tree's output is multiplied by `learning_rate` (also called eta, default 0.3) before it is added. A small rate means each tree fixes only part of the remaining error, like taking small, careful steps. You then need more trees (`n_estimators`), but the model usually does better on new data. Typical final settings are 0.01-0.1 with hundreds to thousands of trees.

**Tree complexity.**

- `max_depth` (default 6): how many questions deep a tree may go. Deeper trees can capture combinations of features but overfit sooner; 3-8 is usual.
- `min_child_weight` (default 1): the least evidence a leaf must hold. For squared error it is simply the number of training rows; larger values stop leaves that describe only a few rows.
- `gamma` (default 0): how much a split must reduce the loss to be made at all.

**Randomness.** `subsample` gives each tree a random share of the rows, and `colsample_bytree` a random share of the features. Values around 0.6-0.9 stop the trees from all copying the same quirks of the data, which reduces overfitting and speeds training up. Set `random_state` to get the same model on every run.

**Regularisation.** `reg_lambda` (default 1) and `reg_alpha` (default 0) shrink the values stored in the leaves, so no single tree can swing a prediction too far.

A practical order: start with a learning rate of 0.05-0.1, tune `max_depth` and `min_child_weight`, then the sampling settings, then regularisation. Finally lower the learning rate, with more trees, for the final model. The code compares accuracy on the training rows with accuracy on the test rows: a big gap means overfitting.
concepts.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from xgboost import XGBClassifier

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=2000, n_features=30, n_informative=8,
                           flip_y=0.1, random_state=0)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)

for params in [dict(max_depth=10, learning_rate=0.3),           # very flexible
               dict(max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.1),
               dict(max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.1, subsample=0.8,
                    colsample_bytree=0.8, min_child_weight=5)]:
    model = XGBClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0, **params)
    model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(round(model.score(X_tr, y_tr), 3), round(model.score(X_te, y_te), 3), params)
# 1.0   0.884 {'max_depth': 10, 'learning_rate': 0.3}   (memorised the training rows)
# 0.994 0.89  {'max_depth': 3, 'learning_rate': 0.1}
# 0.989 0.87  {'max_depth': 3, 'learning_rate': 0.1, 'subsample': 0.8, ...}
# Which setting wins is data-dependent, so always measure on held-out data
takeaways: `learning_rate` and `n_estimators` trade off: lower rate, more trees
`max_depth`, `min_child_weight` and `gamma` control how complicated trees get
`subsample` and `colsample_bytree` add randomness that reduces overfitting
pitfalls: Raising learning_rate to train faster: each tree then takes big steps and the model overfits sooner.

quiz.q: Your model overfits badly. Which change makes XGBoost more conservative?
quiz.explain: A larger min_child_weight requires more evidence per leaf, preventing splits that isolate a few samples.

concepts.name: Missing values and categorical features
concepts.summary: Let XGBoost handle NaN by itself and split directly on pandas category columns, without one-hot encoding.
concepts.why: Built-in handling saves you filling in gaps and making one column per category, and often gives better models.
concepts.body:
**Missing values.** Real data has gaps: a customer who never gave an income, a sensor that failed. Many models refuse rows with `NaN`, so you would first fill each gap with a stand-in such as the column's average. That is called **imputation**, and XGBoost doesn't need it.

Instead, at every split XGBoost learns a **default direction** for missing values. While training, it tries sending the rows with a missing value left, then right, and remembers whichever side reduces the loss more. At prediction time, a missing value simply follows that branch. So you usually should **not** fill gaps for XGBoost: the fact that a value is missing can itself be useful information.

Watch for data that marks missing with a made-up number such as `-999` or `0`. XGBoost would treat it as a real value. Convert it to `NaN`, or tell XGBoost with `missing=-999`.

**Categorical features.** One-hot encoding turns a column such as city into one 0/1 column per city. XGBoost can skip that. Give the column the pandas `category` type with `df[col].astype("category")`, and each split can put a group of categories on each side directly: say Oslo and Rome left, Lima and Kyiv right. In XGBoost 3.x the scikit-learn classes do this by default. Plain text (`object`) columns are refused, so convert them first.

Two settings matter for columns with many different values:

- `max_cat_to_onehot`: below this many categories, each split separates one category from all the rest,
- `max_cat_threshold`: limits how many categories one split may use, to curb overfitting.

The model remembers the categories it saw in training. When predicting, give the column the same list of categories, as the code does with `pd.Categorical(..., categories=...)`.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from xgboost import XGBRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 3000
df = pd.DataFrame({"city": rng.choice(["Oslo", "Rome", "Lima", "Kyiv"], n),
                   "income": rng.normal(50, 15, n)})
y = df["city"].map({"Oslo": 30, "Rome": 20, "Lima": 10, "Kyiv": 15}) + 0.5 * df["income"]
df.loc[rng.random(n) < 0.2, "income"] = np.nan        # 20% missing
df["city"] = df["city"].astype("category")            # split on categories directly

model = XGBRegressor(n_estimators=200, max_depth=4).fit(df, y)

new = pd.DataFrame({"city": pd.Categorical(["Oslo", "Lima"], categories=df["city"].cat.categories),
                    "income": [60.0, np.nan]})
print(model.predict(new).round(1))   # [59.8 34.9] (true: 60.0; Lima with unknown income ~ 35)
takeaways: NaN gets a learned default direction at each split; don't fill gaps by reflex
Use the pandas `category` type to split on categories directly
Give the column the same categories at prediction time
pitfalls: Encoding missing values as 0 or -1, which XGBoost then treats as a real value.

quiz.q: How does XGBoost route a sample whose split feature is NaN at prediction time?
options: Down the default direction learned for that split
quiz.explain: Each split stores the direction that worked best for missing values during training.

concepts.name: Saving and loading models
concepts.summary: Save trained models in XGBoost's own JSON or UBJSON files, which load again in newer versions and other languages.
concepts.why: A model that serves real users must still load months later, after you have upgraded your libraries.
concepts.body:
Training can take minutes or hours, so you save the trained model to a file and load it later, for example in the app that makes live predictions. XGBoost has its own file format for this:

- `model.save_model("model.json")` writes every tree and setting as JSON text. Newer XGBoost versions can still load it, and so can XGBoost for R, Java and C,
- `model.save_model("model.ubj")` writes the same content as **UBJSON**, a compact binary form of JSON: smaller files that load faster,
- `XGBClassifier().load_model("model.json")` loads it back into a fresh model.

The file also stores the extras the scikit-learn class needs, such as the list of classes, so the loaded model works exactly like the original.

Python also has a general way to save almost any object to a file: **pickle**, and `joblib`, a faster version scikit-learn uses. It is the usual choice when the model sits at the end of a scikit-learn pipeline, a chain of preprocessing steps plus the model, because it saves the whole chain at once.

Pickles have two catches. A pickle often won't load after you upgrade the libraries, so record the exact versions you used. And loading a pickle can run code, so only load ones you trust. A common compromise is to save the XGBoost model as JSON and the rest of the pipeline separately.

Always use the `.json` or `.ubj` extension; XGBoost's old binary format is no longer supported. To look inside a model, `model.get_booster().trees_to_dataframe()` lists every tree's splits as a DataFrame.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from xgboost import XGBClassifier

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
model = XGBClassifier(n_estimators=50, max_depth=3).fit(X, y)
model.save_model("iris_xgb.json")            # loads in newer versions too

loaded = XGBClassifier()
loaded.load_model("iris_xgb.json")
print(np.array_equal(model.predict(X), loaded.predict(X)))   # True
print(loaded.classes_)                       # [0 1 2]

trees = loaded.get_booster().trees_to_dataframe()
print(trees["Tree"].nunique())               # 150 (50 rounds x 3 classes)
takeaways: `save_model` to `.json` or `.ubj` loads in newer versions and other languages
Load into a fresh estimator with `load_model`
Use pickle/joblib for whole pipelines only, and record library versions
pitfalls: Pickling a bare XGBoost model and finding it won't load after an upgrade.

quiz.q: Why prefer model.save_model("m.json") over pickle for an XGBoost model?
options: XGBoost keeps its JSON format loadable across versions and languages
quiz.explain: XGBoost promises its own format keeps working in newer versions, whereas a pickle depends on the exact code of the library version that wrote it.

concepts.name: Validation sets and early stopping
concepts.summary: Monitor a validation set during training and stop adding trees when it stops improving.
concepts.why: Early stopping picks the number of trees automatically and is the main defence against overfitting.
concepts.body:
Each **boosting round** adds one more tree. As rounds go by, the error on the training data keeps falling. The error on validation data, rows the model never trains on, falls at first and then starts rising again: the extra trees are learning noise. **Early stopping** watches a validation set during training and stops once its metric has not improved for a set number of rounds.

With the scikit-learn API, set it in the constructor and pass validation data to `fit`:

```python
model = XGBClassifier(n_estimators=5000, learning_rate=0.05,
                      early_stopping_rounds=50, eval_metric="logloss")
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)], verbose=False)
```

After fitting, `model.best_iteration` and `model.best_score` describe the best round, and `predict` automatically uses only the trees up to it. `model.evals_result()` holds the full score history, so you can plot how training and validation error change round by round. If `eval_set` contains several sets, the **last** one is used for stopping.

Rules for doing it right:

- The validation set must be separate from the test set: choosing the number of trees is part of building the model.
- Set `n_estimators` high and let early stopping cut it.
- Inside cross-validation or a hyperparameter search, each fold needs its own validation split; or use `xgb.cv`, which applies early stopping across folds.
- For the final model, either keep the early-stopped model or refit on all the data with `n_estimators` set to around the best iteration (a little higher, for the extra data).
concepts.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from xgboost import XGBClassifier

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=5000, n_features=20, flip_y=0.1, random_state=0)
X_tr, X_val, y_tr, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)

model = XGBClassifier(n_estimators=5000, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=4,
                      early_stopping_rounds=50, eval_metric="logloss")
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, eval_set=[(X_tr, y_tr), (X_val, y_val)], verbose=False)

print(model.best_iteration)                   # 81 (instead of 5000)
hist = model.evals_result()
print(round(hist["validation_0"]["logloss"][-1], 3),   # 0.165 train keeps falling
      round(hist["validation_1"]["logloss"][-1], 3))   # 0.235 validation drifted up
print(round(model.best_score, 3))             # 0.23
takeaways: Set `early_stopping_rounds` and `eval_metric` in the constructor, pass `eval_set` to fit
`predict` uses the best iteration automatically
The validation set is for model selection, not the final test
pitfalls: Using the test set as eval_set, which makes the reported test score optimistic.

quiz.q: With eval_set=[(X_tr, y_tr), (X_val, y_val)], which set does early stopping monitor?
quiz.explain: XGBoost uses the last dataset in eval_set for early stopping.

concepts.name: The native API: DMatrix, train and cv
concepts.summary: Use xgb.DMatrix, xgb.train and xgb.cv for full control, callbacks and memory-efficient data handling.
concepts.why: The native API exposes features and speed the scikit-learn wrapper hides, and it is what the wrapper calls underneath.
concepts.body:
The scikit-learn classes are a friendly layer over XGBoost's own interface, the **native API**. It has three main parts.

**Data.** `xgb.DMatrix(X, label=y, weight=w, missing=np.nan, enable_categorical=True)` is XGBoost's own data holder: the features plus the answers, converted once into the form XGBoost trains on. Building it once and reusing it saves time.

`xgb.QuantileDMatrix` goes further. XGBoost's default way of finding splits never looks at exact values: it first sorts each feature's values into at most 256 ranges, called **bins**, and only tries cut points between bins. A QuantileDMatrix stores just the bin of each value, so it uses far less memory. When you build the validation matrix, pass `ref=dtrain` so it uses the same bins as the training one.

**Training.** `xgb.train(params, dtrain, num_boost_round, evals=[(dval, "val")], early_stopping_rounds=50)` returns a **Booster**, the trained model itself. Parameters go in a dict using native names: `eta` (the learning rate), `max_depth`, `objective`, `eval_metric`, `lambda` and `alpha` (the regularisation settings).

**Predicting.** `booster.predict(dtest)` returns probabilities for `binary:logistic`; there is no separate `predict_proba`. Pass `iteration_range=(0, booster.best_iteration + 1)` to predict with only the best rounds.

**Cross-validation.** `xgb.cv(params, dtrain, num_boost_round, nfold=5, early_stopping_rounds=50, stratified=True)` runs cross-validation with early stopping across folds. It returns a DataFrame of mean and standard deviation scores per round; its length is the best number of rounds.

The native API also accepts `callbacks` (for example `xgb.callback.LearningRateScheduler`, which changes the learning rate as rounds go by), custom objectives, and `xgb_model=` to continue training an existing booster. `model.get_booster()` gives you the booster inside a scikit-learn estimator.
concepts.code:
import xgboost as xgb
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_val, y_tr, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=0)
dtrain = xgb.QuantileDMatrix(X_tr, label=y_tr)
dval = xgb.QuantileDMatrix(X_val, label=y_val, ref=dtrain)   # same bins as train

params = {"objective": "binary:logistic", "eta": 0.05, "max_depth": 3, "eval_metric": "auc"}
cv = xgb.cv(params, xgb.DMatrix(X_tr, label=y_tr), num_boost_round=1000, nfold=5,
            early_stopping_rounds=50, seed=0)
print(len(cv), round(cv["test-auc-mean"].iloc[-1], 4))      # 67 0.994

booster = xgb.train(params, dtrain, num_boost_round=len(cv), evals=[(dval, "val")],
                    verbose_eval=False)
proba = booster.predict(dval)                                # probabilities
print(proba[:3].round(3))                                    # [0.982 0.026 0.026]
takeaways: DMatrix/QuantileDMatrix hold the data; `xgb.train` returns a Booster
Native parameter names differ: `eta`, `lambda`, `alpha`
`xgb.cv` finds the number of rounds with early stopping across folds
pitfalls: Building a validation QuantileDMatrix without `ref=dtrain`, so it uses different bins.

quiz.q: What does booster.predict(dmatrix) return for objective binary:logistic?
quiz.explain: The native Booster applies the sigmoid for you, so binary:logistic predictions are probabilities.

concepts.name: Tuning with scikit-learn tools
concepts.summary: Search XGBoost hyperparameters with RandomizedSearchCV over sensible ranges, without fighting over CPU cores.
concepts.why: Good hyperparameters often make the difference between an average and an excellent boosted model.
concepts.body:
Because `XGBClassifier` is a scikit-learn estimator, the usual search tools work: `RandomizedSearchCV`, `GridSearchCV`, or your own loop driven by an optimiser such as Optuna (a library that picks the next settings to try from how earlier ones scored).

Search ranges that work well:

- `max_depth`: integers 3-10,
- `min_child_weight`: 1-50, sampled log-uniformly (on a log scale, so 1-5 gets as many tries as 5-50),
- `subsample`, `colsample_bytree`: uniformly between 0.5 and 1.0,
- `reg_lambda`, `reg_alpha`: 0.001-10, log-uniformly,
- `gamma`: 0-5,
- `learning_rate`: fix it at 0.05-0.1 during the search and lower it for the final fit.

A random search with 30-100 candidates usually beats a grid of the same size.

Number of trees: either include `n_estimators` in the search with a fixed learning rate, or use early stopping inside each fit. Early stopping inside `GridSearchCV` needs an `eval_set`, which must not be the fold being scored. The clean options are to search `n_estimators` directly, or to run `xgb.cv` for each candidate in your own loop.

XGBoost already uses all your CPU cores by itself, running several threads at once (`n_jobs`). If the search also runs several fits in parallel (`n_jobs=-1`), they fight over the same cores, which is called oversubscription, and everything slows down. Parallelise at one level only.

If the data needs preprocessing, such as a `ColumnTransformer`, put it and the model in a `Pipeline` and search over names like `xgbclassifier__max_depth`. Then preprocessing is refitted in every fold.
concepts.code:
from scipy.stats import loguniform, randint, uniform
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
from xgboost import XGBClassifier

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=2000, n_features=25, n_informative=10,
                           flip_y=0.05, random_state=0)
space = {"max_depth": randint(3, 9), "min_child_weight": loguniform(1, 50),
         "subsample": uniform(0.5, 0.5), "colsample_bytree": uniform(0.5, 0.5),
         "reg_lambda": loguniform(1e-3, 10), "n_estimators": randint(100, 600)}

search = RandomizedSearchCV(XGBClassifier(learning_rate=0.05, n_jobs=4),
                            space, n_iter=25, cv=4, scoring="roc_auc",
                            random_state=0, n_jobs=1)   # parallelise in XGBoost only
search.fit(X, y)
print(round(search.best_score_, 4))                    # 0.932
print({k: round(float(v), 2) for k, v in search.best_params_.items()})
# {'colsample_bytree': 0.96, 'max_depth': 6.0, 'min_child_weight': 1.04,
#  'n_estimators': 358.0, 'reg_lambda': 0.0, 'subsample': 0.86}
takeaways: Random search over depth, child weight, sampling and regularisation works well
Fix the learning rate while searching; lower it for the final model
Parallelise either the search or XGBoost, not both
pitfalls: Passing the CV validation fold as eval_set inside a search, leaking it into model selection.

quiz.q: You run RandomizedSearchCV(n_jobs=-1) over an XGBClassifier that also uses all cores. What is the likely effect?
options: Oversubscribed CPU cores and often slower training
quiz.explain: Both levels try to use every core, so their threads keep interrupting each other.

concepts.name: Feature importance and SHAP values
concepts.summary: Explain XGBoost models with gain-based importance, built-in SHAP contributions and permutation importance.
concepts.why: People affected by a model want reasons, and seeing what drives predictions is how you catch bugs and leakage.
concepts.body:
XGBoost offers several views of what a model relies on.

**Built-in importance**: `booster.get_score(importance_type=...)` with:

- `"weight"`: how many times a feature is used in splits,
- `"gain"`: how much, on average, its splits reduce the loss (the most meaningful of the three),
- `"cover"`: how many training rows its splits affect, on average; plus `total_gain` and `total_cover`.

The scikit-learn wrapper's `feature_importances_` uses gain. These numbers describe the model as a whole, come from the training data, and the different types can rank features differently.

**SHAP contributions**: `booster.predict(dmatrix, pred_contribs=True)` returns, for every row, one exact SHAP value per feature plus a last column holding the starting value every row begins from. For each row they add up to the model's raw output. For a classifier that raw output is the **log-odds**, the score before the sigmoid turns it into a probability: 0 means 50%, positive means more likely yes.

Per-row values explain single predictions ("why was this loan rejected?"), and averaging their absolute values gives a reliable overall importance. `pred_interactions=True` also splits the credit for pairs of features. No extra package is needed, though the `shap` library adds plots.

**Permutation importance** from scikit-learn (`sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance`) on held-out data works for any model and measures the effect on the metric you actually care about.

As with any importance, correlated features share or steal credit from each other, and none of this shows that a feature causes the outcome.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import xgboost as xgb
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes

X, y = load_diabetes(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
model = xgb.XGBRegressor(n_estimators=200, max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.05).fit(X, y)
booster = model.get_booster()

gain = booster.get_score(importance_type="gain")
print(sorted(gain, key=gain.get, reverse=True)[:3])      # ['s5', 'bmi', 'bp']

contribs = booster.predict(xgb.DMatrix(X.iloc[:2]), pred_contribs=True)
print(contribs.shape)                                    # (2, 11) = 10 features + starting value
print(np.allclose(contribs.sum(axis=1), model.predict(X.iloc[:2]), atol=1e-3))  # True

row = dict(zip(list(X.columns) + ["bias"], contribs[0].round(1)))
print(row["bmi"], row["s5"], row["bias"])                # 26.2 20.7 152.1
takeaways: Prefer gain over weight for built-in importance
`pred_contribs=True` gives exact per-row SHAP values that sum to the prediction
Use permutation importance on held-out data to measure impact on your metric
pitfalls: Comparing 'weight' importances across features with very different numbers of unique values.

quiz.q: For a binary classifier, what do the SHAP values from pred_contribs=True add up to for each row?
options: The log-odds score before the sigmoid
quiz.explain: Contributions are on the raw score scale, so they add up to the log-odds, not the probability.

concepts.name: Imbalanced classification
concepts.summary: Handle rare positive classes with scale_pos_weight, sample weights, the right metric and threshold tuning.
concepts.why: Fraud, defaults and failures are rare events, and the defaults optimise for the majority class.
concepts.body:
With a rare positive class, three XGBoost-specific levers help, on top of the general advice to judge the model with precision-recall metrics.

**Reweight the classes.** `scale_pos_weight` makes every positive row count that many times as much as a negative one during training. A common starting value is `n_negative / n_positive`; treat it as a hyperparameter. For more than two classes, or per-row weights, pass `sample_weight=` to `fit` (scikit-learn's `compute_sample_weight("balanced", y)` helps).

Weighting improves how rare cases are ranked in some problems, but it pushes predicted probabilities upward. If you need probabilities you can take at face value (expected losses, risk scores), either don't reweight and tune the decision threshold instead, or recalibrate afterwards with `CalibratedClassifierCV`.

**Watch the right metric.** Early-stop on `eval_metric="aucpr"` (area under the precision-recall curve) or `logloss`, not `error`, which rewards always predicting the common class.

**Steady extreme cases.** `max_delta_step` (for example 1-10) caps how far one leaf may move a prediction. On extremely imbalanced data this keeps the early trees from making huge jumps, so training settles.

Finally, choose the threshold `predict` uses from validation data and your own costs: scikit-learn's `TunedThresholdClassifierCV` works with XGBoost estimators directly. Always split with stratification, so every fold contains positives.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, recall_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from xgboost import XGBClassifier

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20000, weights=[0.99], class_sep=0.8,
                           flip_y=0, random_state=0)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=0)
ratio = (y_tr == 0).sum() / (y_tr == 1).sum()
print(round(ratio))                                     # 99

for spw in (1, ratio):
    m = XGBClassifier(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=4,
                      scale_pos_weight=spw, eval_metric="aucpr").fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    p = m.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
    print(round(average_precision_score(y_te, p), 3), round(recall_score(y_te, p > 0.5), 3),
          round(float(p.mean()), 3))
# 0.467 0.4 0.009   (unweighted: mean probability matches the 1% base rate)
# 0.456 0.54 0.053  (weighted: higher recall at 0.5, probabilities inflated 5x)
takeaways: `scale_pos_weight` ~ negatives/positives is a starting point, not a rule
Reweighting distorts probabilities; tune the threshold or recalibrate
Early-stop on `aucpr` or `logloss`, not `error`
pitfalls: Using scale_pos_weight and then reading predict_proba as true probabilities.

quiz.q: After training with scale_pos_weight=99, the mean predicted probability is 3x the true positive rate. Why?
options: Upweighting positives shifts the model's probabilities upward
The test set is not stratified
quiz.explain: Weighting changes the effective class balance the model learns from, so its probabilities no longer match reality.

concepts.name: Monotonic and interaction constraints
concepts.summary: Force predictions to move in one direction with a feature, and restrict which features may interact.
concepts.why: Constraints build what you already know into the model, often help it on new data, and make it acceptable to regulators.
concepts.body:
Sometimes you know how a feature should act: risk should never fall as debt rises; price should not fall as size grows. An unconstrained model may still learn small reversals from noise. They look wrong to users and can do badly on new data.

**Monotonic constraints**: `monotone_constraints` gives each feature `1` (predictions never go down as it rises), `-1` (never go up) or `0` (no rule). With a DataFrame you can pass a dict: `monotone_constraints={"debt": 1, "income": -1}`. XGBoost then only accepts splits whose two sides respect the order, and passes upper and lower limits down to the branches below. The rule holds for every prediction, with the other features held fixed.

**Interaction constraints**: two features interact when one's effect depends on the other, which a tree captures by splitting on one and then the other further down the same branch. `interaction_constraints=[["age", "income"], ["region", "channel"]]` lets features interact only within each group: a branch that split on `age` may later split only on `age` or `income`. The model becomes closer to a sum of separate effects, which is easier to explain and can reduce overfitting.

Constraints usually cost a little accuracy on the training data and can improve it on test data when they reflect reality. Check them with partial dependence plots, or by sweeping one feature over a range of values on many rows and checking that predictions only move one way.

Both work with XGBoost's default settings and with both the scikit-learn and native interfaces.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from xgboost import XGBRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n = 2000
X = pd.DataFrame({"size": rng.uniform(30, 200, n), "age": rng.uniform(0, 50, n)})
y = 2.0 * X["size"] - 0.5 * X["age"] + rng.normal(0, 40, n)     # noisy

free = XGBRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_depth=5).fit(X, y)
mono = XGBRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_depth=5,
                    monotone_constraints={"size": 1, "age": -1}).fit(X, y)

grid = pd.DataFrame({"size": np.linspace(30, 200, 200), "age": 10.0})
for m in (free, mono):
    pred = m.predict(grid)
    print((np.diff(pred) < -1e-6).sum())   # number of decreases as size grows
# 76 (unconstrained model wiggles down and up)
# 0  (monotone in size)
takeaways: `monotone_constraints` with 1/-1/0 per feature (dict for DataFrames)
`interaction_constraints` lists groups of features allowed to interact
Verify constraints with a sweep or partial dependence
pitfalls: Constraining a feature whose true relationship is not monotonic, which costs accuracy.

options: Debt is the most important feature
Predictions never decrease when debt increases, other features fixed
Debt is used in every tree
The debt coefficient is positive in a linear model
quiz.explain: The constraint enforces a non-decreasing relationship between the feature and the prediction.

concepts.name: Learning to rank with XGBRanker
concepts.summary: Train ranking models for search and recommendations with query groups and NDCG-based objectives.
concepts.why: Search results, feeds and recommendations are judged by order, not by individual scores.
concepts.body:
Think of a search engine. For each search it has many candidate results and must show them in the best order. In **learning to rank**, the training data is a set of **queries** (one search, or one user's visit to a feed), each with several candidate items labelled by how relevant they were (for example 0-4, or clicked/not). Only the order inside each query matters, so only scores relative to other items of the same query count.

`XGBRanker` handles this with:

- `objective="rank:ndcg"` (default), `"rank:pairwise"` or `"rank:map"`,
- a **query id** per row, passed as `qid=` to `fit`. Rows must be **sorted by qid**, so each query's rows sit next to each other,
- `eval_metric` such as `"ndcg@10"` or `"map@5"`, scored per query and averaged. **NDCG** gives 1 for the perfect order and rewards getting the top positions right most.

These objectives learn by comparing pairs of items from the same query: the more relevant one should score higher. `lambdarank_pair_method` chooses the pairs: `"topk"` focuses on pairs that involve the top `lambdarank_num_pair_per_sample` positions, and `"mean"` samples pairs at random. Click data has a catch: people click top results partly just because they are on top, called position bias. `lambdarank_unbiased=True` corrects for it.

`predict` returns scores; sort items by score within each query to get the ranking. Features should describe the query-item pair, such as how well the text matches, how popular the item is, or how much this user liked similar items.

Evaluate with ranking metrics per query, and split train and test **by query** (GroupKFold or GroupShuffleSplit with qid as the groups), so no query appears in both.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import ndcg_score
from xgboost import XGBRanker

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n_queries, per_q = 200, 10
qid = np.repeat(np.arange(n_queries), per_q)             # sorted query ids
X = rng.normal(size=(n_queries * per_q, 5))
relevance = np.clip(np.round(X[:, 0] + 0.5 * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 0.5, len(X)) + 1), 0, 4)

train = qid < 150
ranker = XGBRanker(objective="rank:ndcg", n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.1,
                   eval_metric="ndcg@5")
ranker.fit(X[train], relevance[train], qid=qid[train])

scores = ranker.predict(X[~train]).reshape(-1, per_q)      # 50 test queries x 10 items
rel = relevance[~train].reshape(-1, per_q)
print(round(ndcg_score(rel, scores, k=5), 3))              # 0.946
print(round(ndcg_score(rel, rng.normal(size=rel.shape), k=5), 3))   # 0.538 (random order)
takeaways: Pass `qid` per row and keep rows sorted by query
Use `rank:ndcg` with `ndcg@k` evaluation
Split train and test by query, never by row
pitfalls: Passing rows in random order, so a query's items are not next to each other.

quiz.q: Why must train/test splits for a ranking model be done by query?
options: Items of the same query are related, so splitting rows would leak information
quiz.explain: Ranking is evaluated within queries; mixing a query's items across splits leaks query-specific information.

concepts.name: How XGBoost builds trees
concepts.summary: Second-order gradient boosting, the regularised gain formula, bin-based split finding and splits that handle missing values.
concepts.why: Understanding the method explains what every hyperparameter really does.
concepts.body:
In each boosting round, XGBoost looks at every training row and asks how the loss would change if that row's current prediction moved a little. The answer has two parts: the **gradient** g, which way and how steeply the loss changes (its first derivative), and the **hessian** h, how quickly that slope itself changes (its second derivative, the curvature). For squared error, g = prediction - y and h = 1; for log loss, g = p - y and h = p(1 - p).

The new tree is fitted to these numbers. For a leaf holding rows I, with G = sum of g and H = sum of h, the best leaf value is `w = -G / (H + lambda)`, and the leaf lowers the objective by `G² / (2(H + lambda))`. A split into left and right children therefore has

`gain = 1/2 * [G_L²/(H_L+lambda) + G_R²/(H_R+lambda) - (G_L+G_R)²/(H_L+H_R+lambda)] - gamma`

So `reg_lambda` shrinks leaf values and gains, `gamma` is a fixed price per extra leaf, `min_child_weight` is the smallest H allowed in each child, and `reg_alpha` pulls G toward zero by alpha (to exactly zero when G is smaller than alpha). Leaf values are multiplied by `learning_rate` before being added.

**Split finding**: the default `tree_method="hist"` puts each feature's values into at most `max_bin` (256) bins cut at quantiles, and adds up G and H per bin at each node. Finding the best split then costs time in proportion to the number of bins, not the number of rows. A child's sums are its parent's minus its sibling's, so only one child per split needs counting.

**Missing values**: rows with a missing value are left out of the bins; their G and H are tried on each side of a split, which gives the learned default direction.

`base_score` is the starting prediction for every row; recent versions estimate it from the target.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import xgboost as xgb

X = np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0], [4.0]])
y = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 3.0, 3.0])
params = {"max_depth": 1, "eta": 1.0, "lambda": 1.0, "base_score": 0.0,
          "min_child_weight": 0, "objective": "reg:squarederror"}
booster = xgb.train(params, xgb.DMatrix(X, label=y), num_boost_round=1)

# by hand: g = pred - y = -y, h = 1; left {1,2}: G=-2, H=2; right {3,4}: G=-6, H=2
lam = 1.0
print(-(-2) / (2 + lam), -(-6) / (2 + lam))       # 0.6666666666666666 2.0 (leaf weights)
gain = 0.5 * (4 / 3 + 36 / 3 - 64 / 5)
print(round(gain, 4))                             # 0.2667

df = booster.trees_to_dataframe()
print(df.loc[0, "Split"], round(df.loc[0, "Gain"], 4))   # 3.0 0.5333 (reported without the 1/2)
print(df.loc[1:, "Gain"].round(4).tolist())             # [0.6667, 2.0] (leaf values)
takeaways: Each tree fits gradients and hessians; leaf value = -G/(H + lambda)
`lambda`, `gamma` and `min_child_weight` appear directly in the gain formula
Binning features (`max_bin`) makes split finding fast
pitfalls: Thinking learning_rate only slows training; it shrinks every leaf value, which also acts as regularisation.

quiz.q: In XGBoost's split gain, what role does gamma play?
options: It sets the number of bins
It is the L1 penalty on weights
It is subtracted from the gain, so a split must reduce loss by more than gamma
quiz.explain: gamma is a fixed complexity cost per added leaf; splits with smaller gain are not made.

concepts.name: Custom objectives and metrics
concepts.summary: Optimise your own loss by supplying gradients and hessians, and report custom evaluation metrics.
concepts.why: When the business loss isn't a built-in objective, a custom one optimises what you actually care about.
concepts.body:
Because XGBoost only needs each row's gradient and hessian, you can plug in any loss whose slope and curvature you can calculate.

With the native API, write `obj(predt, dtrain)` returning `(grad, hess)` arrays as long as the data, and pass `xgb.train(params, dtrain, obj=obj)`. `predt` is the **raw margin**: the sum of the trees before XGBoost turns it into a prediction with a **link function** such as the sigmoid. So for a custom classification loss you apply the sigmoid yourself. With the scikit-learn API, pass a function `objective(y_true, y_pred)` returning `(grad, hess)` to the constructor.

Requirements and tips:

- Hessians must be **positive**. If your loss curves the wrong way in places, clip them to a small positive value, or the leaf-value formula -G/(H + lambda) breaks down.
- Set `base_score` sensibly (for example the target mean, or 0 for margins), since XGBoost can't estimate it for a loss it doesn't know.
- Check your gradient numerically on a few points before training.
- With a custom objective, `booster.predict` returns raw margins; apply the inverse of the link (the sigmoid, say) yourself.

Custom metrics: in the native API pass `custom_metric=f(predt, dtrain) -> (name, value)`; in the scikit-learn API pass a scikit-learn style function as `eval_metric=`. It then drives early stopping (lower is better, unless you pass `maximize=True` to `xgb.train`).

Typical uses: uneven costs (running out of stock is worse than having too much), focal loss for imbalance (a log loss that counts easy, already-correct rows less), or log-cosh loss for robust regression (like squared error for small misses, like absolute error for big ones).
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import xgboost as xgb

def asymmetric_sq(predt, dtrain, under_cost=4.0):
    """Squared error where under-prediction costs 4x more."""
    y = dtrain.get_label()
    r = predt - y
    w = np.where(r < 0, under_cost, 1.0)
    return 2 * w * r, 2 * w                 # grad, hess (positive)

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
X = rng.uniform(0, 10, size=(5000, 2))
y = 10 + 3 * X[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, 5, 5000)
d = xgb.DMatrix(X, label=y)
params = {"max_depth": 3, "eta": 0.1, "base_score": float(y.mean())}

plain = xgb.train({**params, "objective": "reg:squarederror"}, d, 300)
custom = xgb.train(params, d, 300, obj=asymmetric_sq)
for b in (plain, custom):
    p = b.predict(d)
    print(round(float((p < y).mean()), 2))   # share of under-predictions
# 0.49  (symmetric loss)
# 0.31  (custom loss biases predictions upward)
takeaways: A custom objective returns each row's gradient and positive hessian with respect to the raw margin
Set `base_score` and apply the inverse link to predictions yourself
Custom metrics can drive early stopping
pitfalls: Returning hessians that are zero or negative, which breaks the leaf-value calculation.

quiz.q: Your custom objective's predt values are on which scale?
options: The raw margin, before any link function
quiz.explain: XGBoost passes raw margins; you apply the sigmoid or another link inside the objective as needed.

concepts.name: GPUs, large data and distributed training
concepts.summary: Train on GPUs with device='cuda', train on data larger than memory, and spread training over many machines with Dask or Spark.
concepts.why: Real datasets outgrow a laptop, and XGBoost's scaling options cut training from hours to minutes.
concepts.body:
**GPU training** is one parameter away. A GPU is a graphics chip with thousands of small cores, and adding up per-bin sums for millions of rows suits it well. `XGBClassifier(device="cuda")` (or `"cuda:1"` for a second GPU) trains on an NVIDIA GPU with the default `hist` method, often 5-20x faster on large data. Keep the data on the GPU when you can (CuPy arrays and cuDF DataFrames are GPU versions of NumPy arrays and pandas DataFrames) to avoid copying between the computer's main memory and the GPU's. A warning tells you when data gets copied at prediction time. The old `gpu_hist` and `gpu_id` parameters have been replaced by `device`.

**Memory** on one machine:

- `QuantileDMatrix` stores bins instead of raw numbers, cutting memory several times over,
- lowering `max_bin` saves memory and time at a small cost in accuracy,
- **external memory**: subclass `xgb.DataIter` to feed data in batches, for example one file at a time. XGBoost first reads every batch to choose the bin edges, then works through the batches again for each tree, so the training data can be bigger than RAM. Combined with GPUs this scales to very large datasets.

**Many machines**: `xgboost.dask` (`DaskXGBClassifier`; Dask is a Python library that spreads work over many cores or machines) and `xgboost.spark` (`SparkXGBClassifier`; Spark is a system for processing data across a cluster of machines) split the rows across workers. Each worker adds up the per-bin sums for its own rows, and the workers combine them (an AllReduce step) so all agree on the same splits. The result is the same kind of model as on one machine. Make sure every worker gets a similar share of the data.

**CPU threads**: `n_jobs` sets how many threads XGBoost uses; leave some cores for loading data. Prediction can be faster too: `booster.inplace_predict(X)` skips building a DMatrix and is safe to call from several threads at once, which suits a prediction server.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import xgboost as xgb

class Batches(xgb.DataIter):
    """Stream data in chunks, e.g. from many files on disk."""
    def __init__(self, n_batches=5):
        self.i, self.n = 0, n_batches
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
        super().__init__()
    def next(self, input_data):
        if self.i == self.n:
            return False
        X = self.rng.normal(size=(20000, 10))
        input_data(data=X, label=(X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] > 0).astype(float))
        self.i += 1
        return True
    def reset(self):
        self.i = 0
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(5)

dtrain = xgb.QuantileDMatrix(Batches(), max_bin=128)    # built batch by batch
print(dtrain.num_row(), dtrain.num_col())               # 100000 10
booster = xgb.train({"objective": "binary:logistic", "max_bin": 128}, dtrain, 50)
X_new = np.array([[2.0, 1.0] + [0.0] * 8])
print(booster.inplace_predict(X_new).round(3))          # [1.] (no DMatrix needed)
takeaways: `device="cuda"` enables GPU training with the hist method
QuantileDMatrix and `DataIter` cut memory and allow data larger than RAM
Use `xgboost.dask` or `xgboost.spark` for multi-node training
pitfalls: Using the removed `tree_method="gpu_hist"`/`gpu_id` parameters from old tutorials.

quiz.q: How do you train an XGBoost model on the GPU in current versions?
quiz.explain: The device parameter replaced gpu_hist and gpu_id; the tree method stays hist.
